None: Um, so let's just go ahead and get started with your background. Maybe tell us a little bit about yourself.

Karthik Narasimhan: Sure, yeah. I'm a professor at Princeton. I've been here for seven years now. I work on broadly research around AI agents just to give a broad term here. But primarily around reinforcement learning and natural language processing, all that. Have been doing that for more than a decade now. I did my PhD back at MIT, and then spent a year at OpenAI. Which was just a really fun time because we actually co-authored the very first GPT paper back then, and it's been crazy to see how that's played out. And yeah, over after that I moved to Princeton. I also spent two years doing a sabbatical at Sierra, which is the new startup that's building agents for the enterprise.

None: Mm-hmm. Awesome. Um, so let's go ahead and start off, uh, way, way, way back when, um, in undergrad. Um, tell us a little about, about kinda your time at IIT Madras.

Karthik Narasimhan: Yeah. So I was in the computer science program at IIT Madras, and one of the things that I remember about, about the whole college experience was like IIT Madras actually has, like, a pretty comprehensive CS curriculum. We learned not just things in AI but also, like, systems theory, all of that. So it was a, it was a really nice environment just to get, like, a very broad base. And I think one of the things that I really enjoyed was the AI classes obviously, and it was as an undergrad where you're very fascinated with programming and stuff, just thinking about machines automating lots of things is, was just, like, mind-blowing to me, right? And I still vividly remember the sort of, the one class that made me really super interested in AI was this intro to AI class taught by was it Bipa Kimani?

He's like a super senior prof. And we had this very nice, like, project where basically we had to build bots. Multiplayer sort of bots for the game of Snake. And it was, like, a whole competition and everything. So it was, like, a lot of fun just beating out other teams. Think, like 10, almost 15 years ago. Like you're building bots to play against each other and all that. But anyway, it was a lot of, a lot of fun. Made me wanna go deeper into AI and, yeah.

It's interesting because I think you sort of come in with grand ideas and passion to do things. Then the first one or two years is literally you just, like, reorienting yourself. You know one of her prior students former students, like, Bronovan, he'd written, like, a really classic paper on, like, how you can use you know NLP to improve RL agents. I think I had all these qualities before, but, like, I cannot emphasize how important that is, right when you're a PhD student and you sort of want to make progress or, like, figure out your niche, right? So I think those, those things are probably far more important than your IQ level or, you know how how you, how you actually, like, how smart you are and things like that.

So anyway, so I think that was the PhD was a really rewarding experience. Started off working on some core NLP tasks. So I'd say when I guess when I started off there was a time of BERT, right? So BERT came out right after GPT, right? Then they took the bidirectional side of things. So I think it was pretty exciting even back then because it was kind of clear that using a transformer, you can go way further than LSTM which were the state of the art back then, right? So I think there was a whole line of looking at how pre-training is evolving. So if you recall, like, that was, that was when the whole pre-training thing evolved, right? Basically, like, you train it on a bunch of, like, raw text, and then you have these parameters that are initialized in such a nice way, right? So I think at that point, I would roughly categorize my interest as like, okay, figure out what's happening with pre-training.

How, how can this apply broadly, not just to NLP? And then the second was on, like, more fundamental problems around, like, RL, like the moral paper and other things where, like, trying to figure out what is missing in RL and what are things that can make it more practical, right? Because if you actually look at the sort of formalization of RL in the classic Sutton and Barto. It's great as a formalism in the theoretical sense. But a lot of things are not really practical, right? So, like, theoretically, yes, you will converge to the optimal policy, blah, blah, blah. But i- in reality, that's so, so far from what you wanna do, right? And for, in fact, for critical applications like, like training a robot. You can't have it destroy itself thousands of times, so. That was kind of the motivation towards what can you do to train these models safely using RL, POLCO, and all of that.

And then I think yeah, and then it was like as these models evolved, right, like the whole scaling paradigm had started. 2019, '20, '21. We were seeing two, three, even the BERT based models were expanding in size and all of that. So I think they were becoming increasingly capable. And it was reaching the point where and it was clear, more and more clear that some of the things that I had wanted to do even back in the PhD. So in text UK, IQN, you can actually think of as like a very rudimentary demonstration of an LLM based agent, right? So it's like it's used the language model to predict things, read text on the text games in RL. But it's, like, very, very rudimentary. It didn't work at all. Like it's like I mean, if you, if you look at that right now, you'll just laugh, right?

It's like, okay, what? But as these models get gone really powerful, right, you have this, like, LLM which has a lot of the right priors. A lot of things change, right? So RL, you don't assume any priors. But with an LLM, you have a lot of the right priors, a lot of the right heuristics. So you can actually do many of these things that we've always dreamt of doing, right? And so it was apparent to me, like, hey, we need to be able to, like, first off, put out the right benchmarks that need to, that need to really push these boundaries, right? So WebShop, for example, was one where, like, yeah, there's a really nice paper by folks at OpenAI. The mini world of this. But it was too rudimentary, too small again, right? So we were like, okay, take this, make it into a realistic task, like shop on Amazon.

Can these models do it, right? And they actually turned out they were not bad, right? So. So I'd say, like, most of the recent stuff for me has been not just to perform research in an isolation, but I think I would actually look at, like, what is something that can have impact. Doesn't have to have immediate impact, but even a few years down the line, right? Something that's more realistic. Let's push the boundaries here, and I think these models are incredibly smart, incredibly capable. I would say even right now, the benchmarks we have are probably a pretty low ceiling for these models. They can do so much more.

Yeah, so I think the flow is really around a fairly consistent question, which is: how do you build systems that can understand language and actually do useful things with it, right? And then I'm pretty flexible about what we need to work on to get there. That's sort of what I meant by not having a predefined arc. You have a direction, but you have to keep updating your ideas about how to make progress.

So a lot of the earlier work was coming at this from the reinforcement learning side. You have an agent, it has to interact with some environment, and it has to learn how to accomplish something. And language is part of that whole process. It could be how you give the agent a task, or it could contain information that helps the agent figure out what to do. That connection was always really interesting to me, going back to the grounding work in my PhD.

And then, as the language models become more capable, the questions you can ask change, right? You start thinking, okay, this thing already has quite a bit of knowledge. How do we get it to use that knowledge when it's making decisions? How do we give it a way to interact with the world? And when something doesn't work, how does it figure out what to do next? So that brings you toward this language agent direction pretty naturally.

But then you also need a way to tell whether you're making progress. And this goes back to the cycle I mentioned. You have an idea for a system, you try it, and then you realize that the tasks you're testing on aren't really capturing everything you care about. So you start asking what a useful task would look like. That's where things like WebShop and SWE-Bench and TAO-Bench fit into the bigger picture.

And the other big part is students. That's one of the reasons I wanted to be at Princeton, right? You can explore several directions with people who bring their own interests and ideas. So the flow is partly the technology changing, partly what we learn from the work, and partly those conversations. I'm always trying to think one or two steps ahead, but you also have to leave room for something interesting that you didn't anticipate.

Yeah, I mean, “go with the flow” makes it sound a little more random than it was. I think the constant throughout has been this question of how do you get language-based systems to actually make decisions and act in an environment? When I started at Princeton, the components were still pretty separate. You had RL agents that could act but were fairly narrow, and language models that could generate text but didn’t really reason, plan, or interact with the world. So a lot of the early work was about building those missing capabilities—exploration, handling multiple objectives, using language as feedback or as a representation for action.

And then the models themselves became much more capable. Once you had large language models, you could suddenly ask a different question: rather than training a policy from scratch for every environment, can the language model itself be the core of an agent? But the moment you try that, you see all these gaps. It needs to reason over several steps, use tools, observe what happened, recover from mistakes. That naturally led to things like ReAct and Tree of Thoughts—different ways of structuring the model’s interaction and reasoning rather than treating it as a system that gives you one answer in one shot.

Then, once those ideas start working, the bottleneck shifts again. You need environments and benchmarks that tell you whether the agent can do something genuinely useful. That’s where things like WebShop, SWE-Bench, and TAO-Bench come in. Software engineering is a particularly nice setting because the tasks are real, the environment is complex, and you can often verify whether the agent actually fixed the issue. SWE-Agent is then the systems side of the same question: given a capable model and a meaningful benchmark, what interface and action space let it operate effectively?

So the flow is really driven by repeatedly asking, “What is the limiting factor now?” Sometimes the answer is a learning algorithm, sometimes it’s a reasoning method, sometimes it’s the agent-computer interface, and sometimes it’s that we don’t have the right evaluation. The surface topics changed a lot over seven years, but to me it has all been one fairly continuous research program around language, learning, and action.

Yeah, so, I mean, I'd push back slightly on the "go with the flow" framing, right? Like, it's, it's not like I'm just drifting wherever the current takes me. I think the way I'd put it is, like, I have a compass but I don't have a map. You know what I mean? Like, the compass has basically been the same thing for fifteen years, which is: language is for doing stuff. It's not, it's not an artifact you analyze in a vacuum, it's, it's how agents coordinate and take actions and learn from each other. So every single thing you just listed, if you squint, it's, like, some version of that question. But the map, like, what's actually tractable, what's the right testbed, what's the bottleneck this year, that changes constantly, and you'd be, like, crazy not to update on that.

So, so concretely, right? When I started at Princeton in 2018, there were no LLMs you could just, like, call. So if you wanted to study agents that use language, you had to build the whole thing yourself, and the honest bottleneck at that point was exploration. Like, we were working a lot with text games, these old, like, interactive fiction games, and the action space is combinatorially insane, right? You have, like, every English sentence as a possible action. And so a bunch of that work, the XTX stuff and so on, is really us banging our heads against, like, "how does an agent explore when the action space is language?" That was, like, a genuinely hard, well-posed problem. And then GPT-3 comes out and, and a big chunk of that problem just, like, evaporates. Not all of it, but the part where you needed the agent to know that "open the mailbox" is a sensible thing to try, that's, that's free now. The prior is in the model.

And I think that's the moment that, like, a lot of the flow happens, right? Because you have a choice. You can keep going deeper on the thing you've built expertise in, and there's, there's a real temptation to do that because you've got students invested, you've got a pipeline, you know the reviewers. Or you can say, "Okay, the ground moved, the interesting question is now somewhere else." And I think the, the single most useful thing I've done as an advisor is being willing to just, like, drop things. ReAct came pretty directly out of that, right? It's, it's a very simple observation once you have a model with a good prior, which is: why are we treating thinking and acting as separate machinery? Just put the thought in the action space. That's, that's kind of it. And, and honestly it's a paper that a 2019 version of me could not have written, not because I wasn't smart enough, but because the substrate didn't exist.

The other huge part of the flow, and I, I really wanna emphasize this because I don't think people outside academia get it, is that the flow is students. Like, genuinely. A lot of what looks like my research direction is, is people like Shunyu walking into my office and being obsessed with something, and my job being to, like, not screw that up. To give them enough structure that it turns into something, and enough room that it becomes theirs. Tree of Thoughts, WebShop, a lot of that, that's, that's not me sitting in a room drawing arrows on a whiteboard. That's, like, taste colliding with taste.

And then the benchmarks thing, that, that was almost forced on us, right? Like, we kept building agents and then sitting there going, "Is this good? I have no idea if this is good." The evaluations everyone was using were, were saturated or they were toy or they were, like, measuring the wrong thing entirely. So SWE-bench, TAU-bench, those come from a very unglamorous place, which is just, like, frustration. We needed a ruler and there wasn't one. And I think that's actually where academia has a real edge right now, honestly, because the labs are, they're optimizing hard against whatever the current measurement is, and somebody has to be willing to go, "I'm gonna spend a year building the thing that tells you your model is worse than you think." That's, like, a weird thing to spend a year on if you're at a company. It's a great thing to spend a year on if you're a professor.

grok.text:
Yeah, so I wouldn’t quite put it as just going with the flow, at least not in the passive sense. I think from the outside it looks like that because there isn’t a pre-defined, like, five-year roadmap taped to the wall. But the destination has actually been pretty stable. Language doesn’t exist in isolation. You shouldn’t solve language in isolation. That’s been true since the PhD, since the grounding work, even since that Snake-bot class, honestly. What changes is what “one or two steps into the future” even means, because the systems themselves keep moving.

When I started at Princeton, we were still in this world where GPT had just shown up and it was, like, a bad poem but a cohesive one, right? Totally different from LSTMs falling off a cliff after a sentence, but still not something you would hand a real job. So a lot of the early faculty work still lived in that RL and language-grounding space. Multi-objective RL, POLCO, XTX — that was still, how do you get agents to actually learn and act when the objective isn’t one clean number, when the world is messy. Same instinct as Text DQN and HDQN, just with a bit more room to explore because now I had students and I could run a few threads at once, which was the whole reason I left OpenAI for academia.

Then the models got good enough that you could start putting language in the loop as the actual control surface, not just as a thing you extract or classify. That’s the ReAct, COM, Tree of Thoughts stretch. Suddenly it’s not “train an RL agent from scratch to play a game.” It’s “the model can already talk, can already somewhat reason — can you get it to act, to plan, to use tools, to not just answer a question and stop.” That’s the same grounding idea, just the substrate changed.

And once that works even a little, the bottleneck moves. It’s not “can it generate text.” It’s “is it doing anything useful.” That’s when you feel the cycle kick in. You need new tasks, not just new methods. WebShop, SWE-Bench, TAO-Bench — that was us saying, look, these things are more capable than Atari, let’s stop pretending the useful version of this is another game. Let’s put them in shopping, in software engineering, in enterprise-style workflows. Then Koala, SWE-Agent, that’s the methods side of the same cycle: okay, we defined the task, now close the gap.

So the flow is really just: look at what the systems can do now, imagine what they should be able to do a couple of years out, and then either build the method or build the benchmark that gets us there. Sometimes that’s RL. Sometimes that’s a prompting or agent scaffold. Sometimes that’s a dataset. I don’t feel the need to pick a camp. And being a professor is what made that possible, because you can work with students across those directions instead of having to bet the whole lab on one.

The Sierra sabbatical is the same instinct, just later in the curve. Agents are capable enough now that you can actually try them in the enterprise, not just in a paper. Still trying to close that gap between what we’re seeing and what’s useful. That’s the through-line. The papers change names. The principle doesn’t.

gemini.text:
Yeah, so I think, you know, from the outside it might look like a bit of a random walk or just going with the flow, but to me, there's always been a very clear unifying thread. And that thread is really: how do we build agents that can reason, take actions, and interact with the world through language?

When I first started at Princeton, like you mentioned, a lot of the initial work was still deeply rooted in reinforcement learning. We were looking at core RL questions—things like exploration, sample efficiency, multi-objective RL, and policy optimization, which led to papers like POLCO and XTX. But in the back of my mind, the goal was always, "How do we connect this decision-making framework back to language?" Because, like I said earlier, language doesn't exist in a vacuum; it's about taking actions and achieving goals.

Then, as language models started getting significantly more capable, the whole landscape shifted. Suddenly, we had these models that possessed a huge amount of world knowledge and broad reasoning abilities, but people were still mostly treating them as passive text predictors or chatbots. So for me, having that RL and grounding background, the immediate question was: "Why can't the language model be the policy? Why can't it be an active agent that takes actions in an environment, observes the feedback, and plans?"

That's really the flow that led to things like ReAct and Tree of Thoughts. With ReAct, it was about intertwining reasoning and acting—allowing the model to think, interact with tools or APIs, observe what happens, and update its thoughts. And with Tree of Thoughts, it was asking how we can get models to explore different reasoning paths and deliberate, almost like a search algorithm.

And once you see that these agents can actually do this, the next natural question in that flow is, "Okay, let's not just evaluate them on standard NLP benchmarks or toy games. What are the hardest, most realistic real-world environments we can put these agents into?" And that pushed us toward things like WebShop, and eventually SWE-bench and SWE-agent, looking at whether these agents can actually act like software engineers and solve real GitHub issues.

So it is a bit of going with the flow, but the flow is really dictated by asking where the frontier is and trying to stay one or two steps ahead. And a huge credit honestly goes to the students in my lab. They come in with great energy and great ideas, and when you give them the space to explore, that flow just naturally evolves into some really exciting directions.

kimi.text:
Yeah, so if I had to actually trace the thread through all of that—and I know I keep saying there's no arc, but I think there is sort of, like, a compass, right, even if there's no map. And the compass has basically always been this idea that language and action are deeply intertwined. Like, language is not just something you process, it's something you use to *do* things.

So the early years at Princeton were really a continuation of that. We were pushing on grounding, getting RL agents to operate in these language-rich settings, text worlds and so on. And the multi-objective RL work came from this realization that real agents in the real world don't have just one nice, clean reward, right? They're juggling multiple, sometimes conflicting objectives. So a lot of those projects in between—COM, POLCO, XTX—were sort of us chipping away at different facets of that same question: how do you make sequential decision-making actually work when things get messy and realistic.

And then I think the big inflection point, honestly, was around 2020 or so, when the language models started getting really good. Because up until then, if you wanted an agent that understood language, you had to teach it language from scratch, right? That was half the battle. And suddenly you're handed these models that come preloaded with all this knowledge about the world. And the question completely changes. It's no longer "how do you learn language," it's "how do you get this thing to actually act in the world instead of just producing text." And that felt like, okay, this is the grounding agenda again, but with a way more powerful substrate.

So ReAct, for instance, came out of this observation that people were doing prompting for reasoning, like chain-of-thought, and separately people were hooking models up to actions and tools, and it was almost obvious in hindsight that those two things should be interleaved—because that's what we do as humans, right? We reason while we act. And Tree of Thoughts was a similar flavor: these models generate left to right, one token at a time, but real problem solving involves exploring, backtracking, considering alternatives. So we wanted the model to be able to do deliberate search over its own reasoning.

And I should say, honestly, a lot of the flow is also just following my students. Like Shunyu, who drove a bunch of this work. Part of the joy of being faculty is you get pulled in directions by what your students are excited about. But yeah, the models keep changing, and the north star's been the same: getting language to actually *do* something in the world. And that leads pretty directly into the agents stuff, which I know we'll get to.

fable.text:
Yeah, so I would slightly push back on the go with the flow, right? Like, I think it's less that I don't have a plan and more that the plan is at the level of, like, a question, not at the level of a method, right? And the question has always been the same. It's basically, how do you build agents that can actually understand language and use it to act in the world? Right? That's been the through line all the way from the Text DQN days. What changes is just what tools you have available to attack that question, and the tools changed, like, dramatically over those seven years.

So when I started at Princeton, the belief was still very much you need RL to get agents, right? Like, that's how you get things that act. But RL had all these problems. It was super sample hungry, it didn't generalize, you'd train something on one text game and it would completely fall apart on the next one. So a lot of those early papers, like the multi-objective stuff, POLCO, XTX, those were all really about, like, how do you make RL less painful? How do you explore better? How do you get some generalization out of these things? XTX for example was literally about exploration in text games, because the agent would just get stuck and never see the interesting parts of the environment.

And then, like, 2020 happens, GPT-3 comes out, and suddenly you have this thing that has, like, a really strong prior about the world just from reading text, right? So CALM was actually sort of the bridge for me. The idea there was, okay, don't make the RL agent figure out from scratch that you can't eat a door. Just use the language model to propose the actions that make sense, and let RL pick between them. So it's, like, the LM is doing the heavy lifting on the commonsense, and RL is doing the decision making.

And then honestly, ReAct was the point where I think Shunyu and I sort of looked at each other and were like, wait, do we even need the RL part anymore? Right? Like, you can just prompt the thing to reason and then act and then reason again, and it works. Which is kind of, kind of humbling if you spent, like, ten years on RL. And then Tree of Thoughts is, like, okay, if the model is the policy, can we put search on top of it? Which is very much, like, classic AI ideas coming back around.

And then the last piece of the flow, and I think this is the part people miss, is at some point the models got good enough that the bottleneck wasn't the method anymore, it was that we didn't have tasks that actually stressed them. Right? Like, ALFWorld and the text games, they were basically solved. So that's really where WebShop and SWE-bench and tau-bench come from. It's not that I woke up wanting to do benchmarks. It's that you can't push one or two steps ahead if you can't even measure where you are.

So, yeah. And I'd also say, like, a huge part of it is the students. Being a professor, half the flow is just, like, someone walks into your office with a crazy idea, and you go, huh, okay, let's try that.
